w: What's tested The basic words: occlusion, articulation, neutral zone, occlusal plane, the curves MIP vs centric occlusion vs centric relation Angle classes and "which cusp hits where" Working, non-working and forward movements; canine guidance and group function What makes back-tooth cusps taller or shorter; vertical dimension; the envelope of motion; articulator parts This first lecture is a review of what you learned last spring, because everything else in occlusion builds on it. Dr. Givan also posted a help sheet called "What cusp hits where?", because those questions show up on every exam and on boards. Basic words Occlusion is how the upper and lower teeth touch when they are still. Articulation is how they touch both still and while the jaw moves. People mix them up, but they are not the same. The neutral zone is the space where the push of the tongue from inside equals the push of the lips and cheeks from outside. Teeth grow into it, and anything you build outside it gets pushed around and tends to fail. The occlusal plane is the average level of the biting surfaces. It is not really flat; it is an average of a curve. Seen from the side, the teeth follow the curve of Spee: from the lower canine tip, along the outer cusp tips of the back teeth, up to the front of the jaw joint. Seen from the front, they follow the curve of Wilson: cupped (concave) in the lower arch and domed (convex) in the upper, because upper back teeth tip outward and lower ones tip inward. For denture teeth, both curves together are called the compensating curve. The sphere of Monson is an old idea that all the cusps sit on a ball about 4 inches in radius, centered near the forehead between the eyebrows (glabella). How the teeth fit Normally the upper teeth's tongue-side cusps and the lower teeth's cheek-side cusps sit in the grooves down the middle of the opposite teeth. These are the centric (holding) cusps: wide and round, about a third of the tooth's width, and they hold up the height of your bite. The other cusps, the non-centric ones, are sharper and about a sixth of the width; they shear food, protect the cheek and tongue, and keep food on the chewing table. In a crossbite the arrangement is flipped. That's fine functionally, and implant crowns often have to be made that way. The upper arch is a bit bigger than the lower (about 128 vs 126 mm long). The chewing table is about half to 60% of a back tooth's width. Contacts between teeth sit toward the cheek side, which makes the gaps on the tongue side bigger, so food falls back toward the tongue. Three positions people confuse MIP (maximum intercuspation) is simply where your teeth fit together best, no matter where the jaw joints are. Your nervous system finds it to protect your teeth, and it changes whenever teeth or fillings change. Centric relation (CR) is a joint position: the jaw joints fully seated, up and forward against the bony bump in front of them (the articular eminence), on the thin middle part of each disc. It doesn't depend on the teeth, you can find it again and again, and from there the jaw can only hinge. Centric occlusion (CO) is how the teeth touch when the joints are in CR. On Dr. Givan's tests, "centric occlusion" always means this, never MIP. In about 90% of people CO and MIP are different, by about 1.25 mm on average; a sideways difference is worse. The CO contact is often unstable, and closing into it (often at night) causes worn spots, cracked cusps and loose teeth. Teeth only touch about 18 minutes a day; the rest of the time the muscles keep the joints seated. Angle classes Class I (about 70%): normal molar fit. "Class I malocclusion" means the molars fit but other teeth are crowded or turned. Class II (about 25%): the lower first molar sits behind the upper. Division 1 has a narrow upper arch and front teeth sticking out; division 2 has a square arch, upper centrals tipped back, laterals flared and a deep bite (hard to restore). Class III (about 5%): the lower first molar sits in front; front teeth are edge to edge or the lower ones are in front. The old Class IV (one side each way) isn't used. If a test question doesn't say the class, assume Class I. Most adults have cusp-to-marginal-ridge contacts (one tooth touching two). The textbook ideal, cusp-to-fossa (one tooth to one tooth), is rare in nature. Which cusp hits where Unless told otherwise, assume Class I and cusp-to-fossa. Draw "fence posts": a row for the upper teeth (canine, two premolars, then front and back halves of each molar) and a row for the lower, with each lower post a half step in front of its upper partner. Class II moves the lower row back a step; Class III moves it forward. The fence tells you which cusp is closest; your tooth anatomy tells you which fossa. For premolars in Class I and III, contacts land in the front (mesial) pits of the upper premolars and the back (distal) pits of the lower ones; Class II is the reverse. Example: in Class I the cheek cusp of #29 sits in the front pit of #4. Front teeth Vertical overlap (overbite) of 3-5 mm is normal, 3 mm is ideal; orthodontists accept about 1 mm to fit braces. Horizontal overlap is "overjet." An open bite is properly an "anterior open occlusal relationship." The shape of the back (tongue) side of the upper front teeth mostly decides the anterior guidance. Moving the jaw The jaw joint hinges and slides, and both sides are one bone, so it is very complicated. Any movement away from the fitted-together position is "eccentric." Moving forward, the joint slides down the bony slope and the back teeth separate (Christensen's phenomenon). If back teeth do hit, the lower teeth's front slopes meet the upper teeth's back slopes. Moving sideways, the side you move toward is the working side (its joint mostly spins); the other side is the non-working or "balancing" side (its joint swings forward and in). Contacts on the non-working side are interferences. To figure out which slopes touch, draw the molars fitted together and move the lower tooth in your head. On the non-working side, the inner slopes of the two holding cusps meet. On the working side, the lower tongue-side cusp meets the upper tongue-side cusp, and the lower cheek-side cusp meets the upper cheek-side cusp. Paths across an upper tooth: forward is toward the front, working is toward the cheek, non-working is toward the front and palate. On a lower tooth they reverse: forward shows up as backward, working toward the tongue, non-working toward the back and cheek. In pictures, the starting contact is at the base of the arrow. Guidance and the ideal Canine guidance: the canines lift the back teeth apart when you move sideways. Group function: a few teeth share the job, useful when the canine is weak, missing or an implant. The guide closest to the teeth has the most effect, so the front teeth matter more than the joints. The ideal: all teeth touching evenly at once, forces straight down the roots, no non-working contacts, and canines or front teeth separating the back teeth. That is mutually protected occlusion: back teeth protect the front teeth when you bite, and front teeth protect the back teeth when you move. How tall can back cusps be? Things that separate the back teeth more allow taller cusps: a steeper joint slope or more vertical overlap. Things that separate them less need shorter cusps: more horizontal overlap, a bite plane that runs parallel to the joint path, a sharper curve of Spee, or more sideways shift of the jaw. For groove direction, everything widens the angle between the sideways paths except a wider distance between the two joints, which narrows it. Bite height VDO is face height with the teeth together. VDR is face height with the jaw resting. The difference, the freeway space, is usually 2-6 mm. Losing back teeth lets the bite collapse (posterior overclosure). The envelope of motion From CR the jaw can hinge open about 20-25 mm; to open wider (40-60 mm), the joints must slide forward. The outer limits of movement are "borders"; teeth limit the top border, and ligaments and joints limit the rest. Posselt drew these limits from the side, from above and from the front, and you should be able to name each line. We almost never use the borders except the top one; chewing happens in a small teardrop shape. The postural position is about 2-4 mm below MIP, held up by a reflex. It is not the same as the position of least muscle activity (about 8 mm down). Head position changes how the teeth meet: sitting up moves contacts forward compared with lying back, so always check fillings with the patient sitting up. The jaw can also shift sideways a little (Bennett movement), measured in millimeters or as an angle. Articulators An articulator is a machine that mimics the jaws and joints. It only helps if it is about the patient's size. Know the parts: upper and lower members, the anterior guide pin and table, mounting plates, condylar elements and the centric latch. Occlusion works in microns: you can feel a hair between your teeth.
